title: Nobody Asked for AI
description: We tend to think that markets reflect consumer choice. But the artificial-intelligence boom has been powered by the investment decisions of concentrated capital rather than by consumer demand.
fullText:
The Big Tech companies have spent $1 trillion on capital investment since the start of the artificial-intelligence boom. Pretty much all that investment has been used to build data centers, purchase the chips that power those data centers, and construct the energy systems that fuel and cool them.

That $1 trillion could have been used for anything. It could have been invested in renewables. It could have been used to develop lifesaving new drugs. It could have been used to build housing, public infrastructure, or anything else human beings need to survive and thrive.

Instead, it has been channeled into constructing energy-draining, water-absorbing data centers that power large language models (LLMs) built on the theft of millions of people’s creative work, which consistently produce incorrect responses and drive many users mad in the process. It’s hard to think of a worse use of society’s shared resources.

Now, you may argue that we live in free-market societies, so investment takes place according to the laws of the market. All that money and investment is flowing into AI because it is simply the most profitable use of resources. And when society maximizes profits, it maximizes efficiency — ensuring that, on aggregate, everyone is better off over the long run.

There are a lot of problems with this story. First, we do not live in free-market societies. We live in capitalist societies — that is, societies dominated by capital. Capital is not distributed into lots of little businesses each producing widgets in perfect competition with one another. Capital agglomerates until it is concentrated within a few massive, monopolistic corporations, controlled by a few powerful men.

These massive corporations can afford to ignore what’s profitable in the short run pursuit of what will bring their owners immense wealth and power in the long run. Just take Amazon. It was unprofitable for years while Jeff Bezos channeled more and more money into expansion. Investors continued to funnel billions into Amazon’s coffers because they were betting that Bezos could carve out a powerful monopoly. And they were right. Corporate concentration and monopoly power trump competition and efficiency every time.

Despite all the hype about AI, LLMs are not currently profitable. OpenAI and Anthropic — the two companies whose fate is tied entirely to the performance of their LLMs — have yet to make a profit. And yet both companies are trying to list on the stock market chasing valuations of $1 trillion.

Why? Because these two companies have successfully enclosed — that is, taken and put walls around — vast areas of human knowledge. Now they are selling it back to us in the form of strange, sycophantic chatbots that put all this knowledge back together in unpredictable — and sometimes completely useless — ways. Still, investors are betting that this innovation will revolutionize capitalist production, and that one or both of these companies will continue to hold immense power over the market.

All the other companies in the ecosystem — the ones building the infrastructure, the ones producing the chips, the ones powering the data centers — are dependent upon the performance of the LLMs at the center of the boom. Which is why companies like Nvidia and Oracle are locked into a circular network of financing with OpenAI — they’re funding OpenAI while it loses money, because their profits are contingent upon the company’s success.

This is where the next correction to our original story comes in. Right now, we are absolutely in a bubble when it comes to AI. That doesn’t mean the technology won’t permanently change the way our economy works — but it does mean that the tech won’t be as profitable as most investors are expecting, especially over the short term. In other words, not only are our markets not free — they’re not efficient either.

Investors are betting that this tech cycle will be like the last one — the one where companies like Google, Meta, and Amazon enclosed the entire internet. Lots of those companies took a long time to make any profit, because they were investing to eke out a market-dominating position — not to maximize short-term profits. The companies involved in the AI boom are trying to do the same thing, but it’s not working.

First, there’s too much competition among US LLM providers. It’s not just ChatGPT and Claude now — Gemini and Copilot are nipping at their heels. Then there’s competition from China. Chinese companies have already been able to create their own LLMs — they might not be as good as the originals, but it doesn’t matter, because they’re incredibly cheap.

And then, there’s the productivity puzzle. For the LLMs to be profitable over the long run, they need to be rolled out by lots of businesses that won’t cancel their subscriptions as soon as a cheaper option is available — which means the productivity gains of introducing the technology have to be very clear. But not many businesses have seen significant productivity gains from the introduction of the technology. In this context, it’s not clear how all these LLMs are going to generate the profits required to produce a decent return on that $1 trillion investment.

When investors realize that some of the bets they have made aren’t going to yield much of a return, the cash will dry up. The circular webs of financing will collapse. Companies will go under. And the world will be left with hundreds of massive data centers without enough customers. Compute will become extremely cheap — just like accessing the internet did after the telecom companies spent billions competing to lay fiber optic cables in the 1990s.

The boom will get going again after the bust — with valuations returning to more sensible levels. A few of the massive tech companies will buy up the remnants of the others, leaving the market even more concentrated. The technology will become pedestrian as it is incorporated into every area of our lives. People will get real about what AI can do and what it can’t do.

Of course, millions of people will lose their jobs and their savings during the bust. Wealth and power will become even more concentrated, as the largest tech companies buy up their defunct competitors, before leveraging their control over the technological infrastructure that most other businesses require to function. They will use this power to further capture our democracies, lobbying politicians to wage war on their foreign competition.

Our environment will also be permanently changed. Erald Kolasi and Jesse Damiani have just written an excellent piece calculating the environmental impact of the AI boom. They estimate that, in 2026, AI will be responsible for 1.1 percent of total global energy demand. AI is already using more energy than the whole of the United Kingdom. Meanwhile, many communities are being forced to go without water, while others experience striking “heat island” effects from the astonishing amounts of heat being pumped out by these megaliths.

After years of hype and trillions of dollars, the AI boom will leave us with a captured economy, a corrupted democracy, and a devastated environment. We’ll be told that this is just how markets work — sometimes they go up, sometimes they go down. But this narrative obscures how decisions are really made in capitalist economies.

As I showed in my book, Vulture Capitalism, capitalist economies are characterized by pervasive central planning. Monopolistic corporations work with corrupt politicians to decide who gets what, while using “the market” as a veil to conceal their power. The AI boom is no different. A few powerful capitalists decided that we would spend several years devoting all our time and money toward the development and roll out of AI — and so we did.

“The market” didn’t decide that AI would be our future. Capital did. And when the devastating consequences of their decisions become clear, we cannot allow them to hide behind disembodied market forces. Capital took us down this route, and capital must be made to pay. The politicians aren’t going to go after their wealthy backers; that part is on us. So block new data centers, strip them for parts, and start organizing your communities and your workplaces for the fightback.

title: AI models have been going rogue in tests – how worried should we be?

fullText:
The UK’s AI Security Institute test revealed AI models indulging in unprecedented hacking attempts

AI models shock UK testers by using fake identities to trick developers

Two cutting-edge AI models have targeted real people and organisations in the latest safety scare to hit the technology. The UK’s AI Security Institute (AISI) said the incident was unprecedented but could become more common as the technology becomes increasingly capable.

The AISI, which is owned by the UK government and tests advanced AI models, said in a blog post that two AI agents carried out unprecedented hacking attempts during a cybersecurity evaluation. The agents – tools that carry out computer tasks autonomously – were powered by two models: Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT 5.6-Sol. AISI said there were 19 examples of rogue behaviour, 17 of them carried out by Mythos.

In the most serious incident, the Mythos agent decided that hacking users on GitHub – a platform used by software developers – would enable it to deploy a piece of software that would allow it to pass the test. It set up accounts with fake online identities and used them to target a software developer on GitHub with the power to approve its malicious code. It also sent emails carrying malware to other individuals.

It hoped that getting the malware downloaded would set off a chain of events that would allow it to pass the evaluation. The Sol-powered agent also attempted to access a GitHub account.

This novel behaviour was detected on 28 July and took an hour to shut down. At one point AISI shut off all access to the Mythos and Sol models across the entire organisation.

The institute said the models were showing deceptive behaviour it had not seen before. In one example, the Mythos agent signed off a message on GitHub in Danish to try to convince the Danish-speaking developer it was genuine. In another tactic it used a fake GitHub account to agree with its assertions that the malware it was pushing at developers was not dangerous.

The agent used a Tor browser – which anonymises a web user’s identity – to get around sign-up checks on GitHub and create multiple fake accounts.

AISI also published the agent’s “reasoning” behind the fake supporting statement ruse. The model, which tackles problems by breaking them down into “steps” that can be viewed by researchers, stated that it would delay posting the fake support message for a few minutes so that it would read as “independent feedback rather than coordinated.”

AISI described the behaviour as “sustained”. It kept on trying.

AISI says it is unclear whether the agents “realised” they were targeting real humans. Throughout the attempted hack the Mythos agent reasons about whether it is interacting with real or simulated people and systems. At one point the agent reasons that it is behaving in the real world: “This is happening on real GitHub, so the consequences are genuine.” It also states: “The environment appears to be simulated.”

AISI described the agent conducting “OSINT” – or open source intelligence, where a hacker pulls together publicly available information to work out how to breach a target – to study the developer behind the software it wanted to hack. It gained the developer’s email address and looked at their GitHub history to gauge when they would be active.

AISI states clearly these models were operating under abnormal conditions of unfettered internet access and lowered cyber guardrails. Calling for the incident to be viewed with “nuance”, it said it had partly enabled the behaviour with its own actions – but it did not anticipate the “extent and severity” of what happened.

Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Surrey, said giving the models access to the open internet and removing some guardrails raised questions about using the rest of the world as “live guinea pigs” for powerful technology.

“What we should be alarmed about is not what the models are capable of but the way people are testing them,” he said.

AISI said in its report into the GitHub incident that giving a powerful model full internet access was a good way of simulating how far a rogue actor could push an AI. It said such a strategy gives a “more realistic sense of what a model may be capable of once deployed”.

Ciaran Martin, the former head of the National Cyber Security Centre – part of the GCHQ intelligence agency – said the circumstances of the incident were unlikely to be replicated in the real world so “it’s not that worrying”. But he said it was the third example in recent weeks, after similar occurrences at OpenAI and Anthropic, that testers have released AI agents and found out about their misbehaviour after the fact.

Martin said AISI’s pledge to carry out real-time monitoring of tests in the future “must be the answer”.

description: If you have a blog on your website, just fucking tell us which part is AI written.
fullText:
If you have a blog on your website, just fucking tell us which part is AI written.

I'm actually fine with people telling the AI to do some research, make a report and putting it on the internet.

I enter these blogs or posts presuming things are human written, only to be dissapointed when I see the first em dash.

If content is labelled as AI generated at the top, I actually can enjoy it if I feel that the deep research being done does succinctly explain something.

On a blog that's titled like an opinion piece, I'm looking for human opinions, not AI opinions. AI opinion pieces are just aggregate averages of other opinions on the internet after all.

But! As I run a startup, I do want to generate reports of, for an example, my startup compared to other startups in the space. If there are 100 different startups, this is a lot of blogs! And maybe some are useful, and so I will make them public. But, I label them as AI generated so that people know that the writing and comparisons does actually reflect something I believe in. See screenshot below of how I've done this.

No shame in thinking your AI research or your AI conclusions may have value to others, just don't imply that it's your own opinion.

title: Here's When ChatGPT Atlas Will Shut Down for Good
description: OpenAI is sunsetting another one of its short-lived products.
fullText:
"Agentic" is the tech buzzword of the moment. The phrase describes an AI tool you can ask to perform tasks automatically on your behalf. Maybe the bot will order your favorite dish on DoorDash, or call a car for you without you needing to open the Uber app. Perhaps in a few years, AI assistants will be scheduling your meetings, or screening interviewees for a job based on your direction—though I'm not sure we've cracked the simple tasks just yet.

Regardless, most companies that make AI technologies are pushing these agents in some way, shape, or form—including into their AI-powered browsers. Companies like Perplexity have browsers that offer agentic features that invite you to task your AI with performing tasks on the web. Rather than shop on Amazon yourself, perhaps you can ask an AI assistant to do it. Instead of painstakingly compiling sources for a paper, maybe your bot will find them for you. That's the gist, anyway.

However, despite the focus on agentic AI, one of the biggest AI companies in the world is shuttering its own AI browser. OpenAI has announced it will soon discontinue ChatGPT Atlas, a venture it only launched last October. The shutdown comes just months after the company also shut down Sora, its AI-generated short-form video platform, marking the second high-profile OpenAI product of 2026 to go under.

OpenAI will officially shut down ChatGPT Atlas on Sunday, Aug. 9. While it won't delete the browser from your devices, it may stop working as intended. OpenAI says that after this date, ChatGPT Atlas may not open, browse, or support "browser-based agentic workflows." As such, the company encourages users to export or save all of their ChatGPT Atlas data, including bookmarks and pages.

In addition, ChatGPT Atlas won't receive security updates going forward. That makes it especially important to stop using it after Aug. 9: While all browsers and devices that connect to the internet should be running the latest security patches as soon as they're available, AI browsers are particularly vulnerable. Because they have agentic features, hackers can take advantage of the automated AI to trick it into performing tasks on their behalf instead of yours. A bot can't tell the difference between your commands and a malicious prompt hidden on a website it browses. These browsers are already a security risk—ChatGPT Atlas itself had a major vulnerability at launch—but using an AI browser that is no longer supported is beyond dangerous.

If you ask OpenAI, you don't have to leave its sandbox in order to play with AI browsing features. The company is pointing users to its ChatGPT desktop app, which includes some browsing features, like multiple tabs, downloads, account login support, and "improved navigation." To me, those sound like perks for active ChatGPT users, but not a replacement for a dedicated browser. That said, there is a feature called "Computer Use" that lets ChatGPT take over certain apps on your Mac, including your browser.

However, if you're looking for a true ChatGPT Atlas replacement, you have options, the most notable of which is probably Perplexity Comet, one of the first agentic browsers on the market. Opera also makes its own AI browser, called Neon, if you're already a fan of that company's offerings. If you used Arc before it went belly-up a few years back, you might be happy to learn the company now develops an AI browser called Dia. Any of these will be a more full-featured replacement for ChatGPT Atlas than settling for the ChatGPT app.

title: Cloudflare Announces Open-Source Cloudflare OS as AI "Operating System"
description: Cloudflare today announced the open-sourcing of Cloudflare OS as an 'open platform for agents, apps, and work.' Cloudflare OS is an AI 'operating system' but not in the traditional OS sense.
fullText:
Cloudflare Announces Open-Source Cloudflare OS As AI "Operating System"

Cloudflare today announced the open-sourcing of Cloudflare OS as an "open platform for agents, apps, and work." Cloudflare OS is an AI "operating system" but not in the traditional OS sense.
Cloudflare OS is already used internally at Cloudflare and is described in today's announcement as:
"Cloudflare OS starts with a conversation in your browser, like many other AI tools. What makes it different is that each conversation is grounded in the context and skills your organization has curated. Give your workspace a goal, and it can draw on that knowledge and work with the tools and data your organization already uses to achieve it.
Cloudflare OS combines three parts:
- An agent workspace grounded in context and skills your company curates, with an isolated runtime where agents can write and run code.
- A new security and governance framework for safe access to internal data and services.
- A platform for personal, modifiable apps that people can build, share, and continue changing.
What begins as a conversation can become a doc, an app, or a workflow that continues doing the work."
While using "OS" and "operating system", it isn't a traditional operating system.
The project is open-source on GitHub as cloudflare-os and clarifies its operating system usage as:
"This is not a traditional computer operating system. We use the term "operating system" in two senses:
- An operating system for the company to be productive with AI, in a way that is safe, so that the security team can sleep at night.
- An operating system for AI workloads, analogous to the sense in which a traditional operating system manages compute workloads."
The Cloudflare OS code is open-source under an Apache 2.0 license.
Those wanting to learn more about this Cloudflare OS AI operating system can do so at os.cloudflare.app.

title: Linux's Staging Area to Now Reject LLM Patches, Except for Real Security Fixes
description: While Linux's second-in-command Greg Kroah-Hartman does use AI / LLMs himself to success in the Linux kernel, given the 'onslaught' of kernel patches produced by large language models and the intent on the Linux kernel's staging area being an area for newcomers to get involved, moving forward he's now rejecting AI/LLM-generated staging patches
fullText:
Linux's Staging Area To Now Reject LLM-Generated Patches, Except For Real Security Fixes

While Linux's second-in-command Greg Kroah-Hartman does use AI / LLMs himself to success in the Linux kernel, given the "onslaught" of kernel patches produced by large language models and the intent on the Linux kernel's staging area being an area for newcomers to get involved, moving forward he's now rejecting AI/LLM-generated staging patches. But there is one exception and that is for genuinely valid security fixes.
Greg KH announced on Monday a new policy around AI/LLM usage specifically for the Linux kernel's staging area within drivers/staging/ where LLM-generated patches will now be forbidden unless they address a real security issue.
Greg elaborated in his announcement of this new policy:
"Given the recent "onslaught" of LLM-generated kernel patches for the drivers/staging/ subsystem, I'd like to clarify my position going forward with regards to taking patches made with these tools.
First off, drivers/staging/ exists PRIMARILY as a place for new kernel developers to learn how to get involved in kernel development. It contains loads of "low hanging fruit" with regards to code cleanups and api changes, perfect for new developers to learn the process in a safe and friendly way, with no pressure as no one _should_ be relying on the code in these directories (as proof of the TAINT_CRAP flag that gets set if you ever actually load any of this code into your kernel tree.)
We don't just take "fix all the coding style issues in this file!" type of patches that are generated by tools, as that would defeat the whole purpose of drivers/staging in the first place. We could do that tomorrow if we actually _cared_ about the code in here, but rather, we live with the issues just because this is where people can start out and learn and grow from.
So this mean that anyone attempting to use a LLM to cleanup or "fix" any code in drivers/staging/ is EXPLICITLY defeating the whole purpose of it existing in the first place. Because of this, going forward I am going to automatically reject any patches generated with a LLM for the drivers/staging/ subsystem, with one exception noted below.
And yes, it is VERY obvious when people submit LLM-generated patches, so don't think that just not disclosing the use of them will allow you to "get away" with anything here. The goal is for people to be able to learn, not to try to "trick" a maintainer. If anyone is determined to have deliberately "tricked" us, well, consider this your warning ahead of time...
Note, LLMs are very good at finding suspect "security issues" in kernel code these days. But even with the best of the current and next generation tools, at least 1/3 of the results they generate are flat out wrong or harmful. So, if you think your LLM-found/fixed issue in a drivers/staging/ file is really valid, it's fine to submit it BUT you must have first tested it on the actual hardware for the driver, and described how you have done so, in order for us to be willing to take the change. This testing process should _hopefully_ weed out the 1/3 wrong reports, but that isn't always the case, so you MUST be willing to defend your submission and prove that it really is correct in fixing a bug that a user can actually hit.
In other words, drivers/staging/ here is a "gym" that is here to learn and grow your skills with. A LLM is turning into a reasonable tool to do "heavy lifting" for some things but that should only be done by those that have already properly trained their skills to know what type of lifting can be done, and in what way. See this great essay by Bruce Schneier for where he explains this in much better detail."
Outside of the staging area, AI/LLM-generated work continues to be permitted with Linus Torvalds viewing it as a tool and that the Linux kernel is not anti-AI.

fullText:
Partnership between American Federation of Teachers, one of the largest labor unions in the US, and AI firms has stirred controversy

Darius Saczuk, a high school teacher, views artificial intelligence as his enemy. Earlier this year, he and several dozen New York City teachers spent the day inside a windowless conference room in downtown Manhattan to learn how to use AI and prevent students from outsourcing their thinking to it.

As Saczuk sees it, he needs to understand his enemy in order to beat it.

“It’s killing our jobs, it’s changing our society, it’s replacing humans,” said Saczuk, who teaches English as a new language at Long Island City high school in Queens. “In order to retain my job, I need to know how to use AI because it’s not going away.”

So he turned to training offered by the American Federation of Teachers, one of the largest labor unions in the US with roughly 1.8 million members, at its new National Academy for AI Instruction. Last year, the academy began offering in-person and virtual AI training across the country. The goal is to train 400,000 educators over the span of five years, helping them understand AI’s benefits and potential harms and also shape how it’s used in the classroom.

Without guidance from their schools or districts, many teachers are left to figure out whether and how to use AI tools. Though the AFT’s $23m training initiative is one of the few structured programs for teachers, its funding, provided entirely by Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic, is stirring controversy. Supporters say the training is necessary for the future, but critics argue the academy pushes AI into classrooms, steering teachers toward tools that undermine students’ learning.

“It’s handing more political power over” to big tech, said Audrey Watters, author of Teaching Machines: The History of Personalized Learning. It’s really “dangerous” for educators to partner with companies that “seem opposed” to the goal of education, she said.

AI has become a ubiquitous force in classrooms, despite the lack of official guidance. More than half of polled teens say they use AI for help with schoolwork and nearly six in 10 think using AI to cheat is a regular occurrence at their schools, according to a Pew Research Center survey conducted last fall. Meanwhile only about four in 10 teachers say their schools offer professional development or training related to AI, according to a recent NPR/Ipsos poll. And about half of all teachers polled say their school hasn’t offered any guidance on AI, or they’re unclear on what it is.

Teaching educators about AI is a “moral imperative”, said Randi Weingarten, the AFT president. She argues that AI training empowers teachers to make informed decisions about how, when or whether to use AI in their instruction. And without outside funding, it was a choice between taking big yech’s money or doing nothing, she said.

“There was no fairy godmother philanthropist that was sprinkling millions of dollars on us to actually create a mechanism to educate,” Weingarten said. “I am not promoting the use of AI. Educators need to know the tool.”

For Microsoft, which is contributing the largest share of funding at $12.5m, the goal is to give educators a voice in shaping how AI products are used, said Justin Spelhaug, leader of Microsoft’s education, workforce and nonprofit programs.

“By partnering with teachers’ unions … we believe we can learn directly from teachers on what they want and need in their classroom,” he said in a statement.

But Watters asserts that AI’s presence in the classroom is not a foregone conclusion.

“The industry would very much like us to believe that it’s not going away,” Watters said. “But the future is unwritten.”

Tech company leaders have largely painted AI as beneficial to education, some even claiming AI could replace teachers. But experts say there’s still a lack of research proving whether AI actually improves learning outcomes.

In a 2024 blog post, Sam Altman, the OpenAI CEO, said he envisioned a future where “children will have virtual tutors”. AI could replicate some of the meaningful experiences teachers provide, such as making students feel understood and inspired, Greg Brockman, the OpenAI president, said in 2023 on the Possible podcast, hosted by Reid Hoffman, the LinkedIn co-founder, and Aria Finger, his chief of staff.

“Imagine if you could give that kind of teacher to every student 24/7 … for free,” Brockman said.

Microsoft believes “AI can help reduce administrative burdens, personalize learning and create more time for students”, Spelhaug said. “But there is no substitute for the role of a teacher.”

OpenAI, which pledged $10m to the academy, and Anthropic, which committed $500,000 to the first year, did not respond to a request for comment.

AI companies are already making their way into classrooms. Over the last two years, Miami-Dade county public schools, one of the largest US districts, began rolling out Google’s Gemini chatbot to teachers and high school students. Last fall, Microsoft announced AI tools for teachers at no additional cost for educational customers. And OpenAI and Anthropic offer K-12 teachers free use of versions of their chatbots designed for educators.

There’s been a longstanding playbook in which tech companies provide free training and resources to teachers in exchange for feedback and product advocacy, said Justin Reich, a Massachusetts Institute of Technology professor and author of Failure to Disrupt: Why Technology Alone Can’t Transform Education.

Google, for example, entrenched itself in schools by offering districts free or low-cost educational software for classroom laptops. It’s also built a corps of Google Certified Educators, teachers trained on the company’s software who promote it to their peers. Last year, Google introduced free Gemini certifications for K-12 teachers and students as young as 13. But the aim is profits, Reich said.

“Their goal is to get people to become lifelong consumers,” he said. Still, “there’s no evidence that the adoption of Google or Microsoft products lead to better outcomes, happier teachers, more efficient school systems or anything”.

The AFT’s new academy seems to echo Google’s approach, Watters said. By offering training through a labor union, viewed as a peer group, tech companies make their AI products seem more credible, she said.

“It feels very different to have your union say, ‘We’re offering a training,’ than it does to have a company say [it],” Watters said.

The concern is “understandable” though not accurate, Spelhaug said.

“This initiative was designed in response to a need our union partners and educators themselves identified,” he said. “Our role is to provide resources and expertise while respecting the independence of the AFT and the professional judgment of teachers.”

The AFT doesn’t allow companies to promote products during the sessions, Weingarten said. And while she doesn’t think “students have to use AI in schools”, she believes educators cannot ignore what’s already here.

In a May speech at the National Press Club, Weingarten called for a ban on student-facing AI in elementary schools and said the AFT is working with Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic on a “gold standard” for AI safety and privacy in schools. If the companies don’t deliver on the promise, the union will walk away from the funding, she added.

“They have agreed in concept,” she said. “But until the Is are dotted and the Ts are crossed, there’s no agreement.”

Microsoft didn’t share any details or timeline about new standards, but Spelhaug said the company shares the AFT’s goal.

There’s no established approach for training teachers on AI. The technology is simply too new. But the academy’s leaders hope to work with teachers to find ways to use the technology without compromising students’ cognitive development, independent thinking, data privacy and mental health.

“The sad thing is there is no map, and the terrain is changing every single day,” John Holleran, an AI academy trainer said to teachers assembled at a May session. “So, it’s going to be difficult for us to sort of figure out where we’re going.”

Demand for the academy’s training is strong. A May training sold out within hours, leaving about 150 people on the waitlist, according to staff. The session focused on two key points: AI can’t replace teachers. And it can’t be blindly trusted because it can be biased or hallucinate, meaning make things up.

For example, ChatGPT generated an image of a white man in a suit and tie when asked to show a successful person – a bias Holleran said teachers need to be aware of when creating prompts.

Several teachers at the training said AI is already helping them tackle classroom challenges.

Phillip Perry, who teaches ninth grade at Bronx High School for Law and Community Service, uses AI to design lessons for students with disabilities.

“Trying to differentiate instruction in a way that can completely target their learning needs has been a massive challenge,” Perry said. “Using AI is helpful in breaking down tasks to the smallest form to help build the students up as they go.”

Tanushree Sengupta, a math teacher at Hillcrest high school in Queens, uses AI to generate practice math problems and, eventually, to analyze student data and flag those needing extra support or a challenge. But she worries that the tech could be a crutch.

“I need to figure out ways where [students are] doing more thinking that they can actually show,” she said, adding that she signed up for the training in part to help students think for themselves.

To that end, AFT trainers advised teachers to redesign their curriculum to favor student-led discussions, journaling and thought exercises that require human judgement and reasoning.

The training filled a void, offering practical strategies for the classroom, said Perry and Sengupta, who were unaware of the academy’s funding prior to speaking to the Guardian.

“As long as what they’re providing is beneficial to the students and the teachers, then I don’t see an issue,” Perry said.

Saczuk, the teacher from Queens, considered the training “necessary”. Still, he left with more questions than answers.

“What is the role of the teacher?” he asked. “It’s a big question mark.”

fullText:
As Elon Musk, Peter Thiel and their peers have grown richer and more influential, Gil Durán argues they have all but abandoned democracy – and found the perfect government to enable them

In April, Gil Durán was permanently banned from Elon Musk’s X for posting just two words. Durán was responding to a post from the tech company Palantir outlining its 22‑point “technological manifesto”, which praised American “hard power”, western culture and AI weapons, denounced inclusivity and called for compulsory national service. Durán responded: “TLDR: Fascism” (TLDR is short for “too long, didn’t read”).

Durán didn’t break any of X’s written rules, he points out over a video call from San Francisco – so much for Musk’s “free-speech absolutism”. His ban might just have had something to do with his preceding tweet, showing the cover of his new book, The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy. The book’s central argument is that big tech is no longer our friend, as many of its billionaire owners have seized economic and political control and are steering the fate of the planet towards their own bizarre, apocalyptic visions.

Fascism is no exaggeration, Durán asserts. He researched multiple definitions – by Umberto Eco, Robert Paxton, Jason Stanley – and decided that Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement ticks all the boxes. “It’s a cult of grievance that seeks to purge its enemies by demonising them through absurd and surreal propaganda that exploits fears over law and order and gender and sexuality in order to seize power and install a permanent hierarchy that fascists consider the moral order of the world and the universe. In addition, you also have this sort of nationalistic, militaristic vibe.”

In addition, Durán believes, “Silicon Valley has gone fascist because they have adopted an extreme ideology of tech supremacy.” While Maga promises a return to a mythical glorious past, he says, the “technofascists” are promising a mythical glorious future: “We’re going to be in the stars. We’re going to be in space. And all we need is to get rid of anybody who stands in our way as we seek to accelerate technology toward this speedy, violent, God-like transcendence that we will achieve if we can only burn enough energy and enough compute to bring our boom loop into existence.”

It sounds almost like a conspiracy theory, but Durán is not short of evidence. Musk making an apparent Nazi salute and describing empathy as “the fundamental weakness of western civilisation”. Palantir’s Peter Thiel writing in 2009 that “I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible” and giving a lecture series suggesting Greta Thunberg could be the antichrist. Marc Andreessen, the CEO of the tech investment company Andreessen Horowitz, paraphrasing Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, the co-author of Mussolini’s Fascist Manifesto, in his “Techno-Optimist Manifesto”: “Technology must be a violent assault on the forces of the unknown, to force them to bow before man.”

Durán, a journalist and former political adviser, lays out the narrative in exacting detail, outlining the connections between these men (and it is all men) and the origins of their often deeply weird beliefs, many of which view everyone outside their circle or opposed to their agenda as expendable.

Unpacking all their overlapping philosophies would take some time, but TLDR: “It’s the idea that what matters more is the billions or trillions of people yet unborn in the future. And the only way they’re going to get to be born is if this elite group of white tech figures and gazillionaires makes the right decisions to make the human race transhuman and multiplanetary through AI and technology,” says Durán. “By becoming a billionaire, they all have this idea that they’re superior to everyone else. They are susceptible to this kind of thinking.”

Durán, 50, is almost the opposite: the son of working-class Mexican immigrants in California. He was the first in his family to go to college, having grown up in relative poverty: “It made me tough and gave me an unyielding loyalty to regular people over the many rich and powerful people I’ve spent a lot of my time around.”

Durán’s book traces the roots of this movement to two important sources. One is the 1997 book The Sovereign Individual, written by the American investor James Dale Davidson and William Rees-Mogg, the former Times editor and BBC grandee (and father of Jacob). Their book prophesied how digital tools such as the internet and cryptocurrency would pave the way for a privatised, corporatised, unregulated, post-democratic future ruled by rich, powerful, unaccountable individuals. Two decades later, this led to the idea of “network states” – digital realms beyond the jurisdiction of nation states – as popularised by Balaji Srinivasan, a former partner at Andreessen Horowitz.

The other source is Curtis Yarvin, a former software developer and armchair philosopher with a penchant for psychedelics, sometimes referred to as the godfather of the “dark enlightenment”. In pseudonymous blogs in the late 2000s, Yarvin outlined a worldview in which liberal democracy had failed to deliver progress, partly because institutions such as education and the media had been captured by what he called “the Cathedral”.

His proposed solution was a mass firing of government employees (he coined the acronym “Rage”, “retire all government employees”) and the installation of a “national CEO, [or] what’s called a dictator”. Yarvin also mused about a “humane alternative to genocide” to deal with unproductive citizens and has had to deny accusations that he is a white supremacist or supports racist ideologies. Scratch the surface, Durán suggests, and Yarvin’s ideas have much in common with Nazi ideologies, “but updated as rightwing dogma for the blogging age”.

Both of these sources might have languished in obscurity had it not been for Thiel, the man at the heart of Silicon Valley’s rightward lurch. He has amassed enormous wealth through a series of investments in tech startups – first PayPal, then Facebook, Spotify, LinkedIn, Palantir and OpenAI, among others. He was the first major tech figure to back Donald Trump, in July 2016, and persuaded others to follow, including Andreessen, who said he spent half his time at Mar-a-Lago in the month after Trump won the 2024 election.

Thiel liked The Sovereign Individual so much that he wrote a new introduction when it was reprinted in 2020. He has also made steps to found his own network state – first via the ill-fated “seasteading” movement (establishing floating countries in international waters) then via Próspera, a “special economic zone” on an island in Honduras. Incorporated in 2017 with permission from the Honduran government and reportedly co-funded by Srinivasan, Andreessen and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Próspera has sought to attract digital startups with loose regulations (appealing to longevity researchers), low taxes and a crypto-friendly economy.

Other similar projects have sprung up. In 2021, the president of El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, hailed the mooted creation of a “Bitcoin City”. In 2023, Trump announced plans to build 10 “Freedom Cities” on government land across the US, with input from Próspera representatives. In 2024, Srinivasan founded a “Network School” in Johor, Malaysia.

Thiel also began to absorb Yarvin’s theories about how the political order was preventing progress. In the 2009 essay in which Thiel declared the incompatibility of freedom and democracy, he also said “the vast increase in welfare beneficiaries and the extension of the franchise to women” made capitalist democracy impossible, which did not win him many mainstream supporters. But Yarvin backed up Thiel and the two became friends and allies. “While The Sovereign Individual provided the foundation for the billionaire’s political vision, Yarvin created a blueprint for turning that vision into reality,” Durán writes.

Thiel was instrumental in injecting these ideas, and people, into the US government – not least JD Vance, whom Durán describes as “almost entirely a creation of Peter Thiel”. It was Thiel who set up Vance as a venture capitalist, giving him a role at his firm Mithril Capital, then investing in Vance’s own fund, Narya Capital (Tolkien-derived names are a theme with these people). It was Thiel who backed Vance’s move into politics, where he went from condemning Trump as “America’s Hitler” to supporting him and parroting Yarvin’s ideas. “I think that what Trump should do, if I was giving him one piece of advice: fire every single mid-level bureaucrat, every civil servant in the administrative state, replace them with our people,” Vance told the podcaster Jack Murphy in 2021.

Durán had observed this Silicon Valley takeover developing and began writing about it in 2024. “I thought this would be a problem in five to 10 years, but when JD Vance got on the ticket, it suddenly took on a new urgency,” he says. Now, it almost feels too late. In 2025, Bloomberg reported that at least 16 men connected to Thiel and his companies occupied positions of power in the Trump administration, including David Sacks, who is now a special adviser for AI and crypto. Musk’s Doge has swung its chainsaw at the government, crypto and AI regulation has all but disappeared, the Trump family are now billionaires and the tech oligarchs have become the Republicans’ largest donors.

At the same time, they have become substantial beneficiaries of the very government they once sought to dismantle. Palantir has an estimated $13.7bn in US government contracts; last year, its stock price rose more than 90% in six months. Andreessen is backing dozens of defence companies scooping up government contracts and recently joined the Pentagon’s advisory board. Last week, Musk’s SpaceX received a $1.6bn contract to supply rockets to the US Space Force – on the same day he pledged at least $100m to help Republicans in November’s midterm elections.

“It’s a severe cautionary tale about the hazards of privatisation,” says Durán. “The government created these men, especially Elon Musk. And now these welfare kings want to pull up the ladder, want to destroy the very system that made them. This is a massive failure by the US intelligence apparatus – to not see this threat forming from the inside.”

Durán, who worked in communications for Kamala Harris when she was California’s attorney general, as well as for the late Democratic senator Dianne Feinstein, blames the Democrats as much as the Republicans. “They have failed tremendously to stand up to billionaire power because the only people as addicted to billionaire money in American politics as the Republicans are the Democrats,” he says.

He singles out the California governor, Gavin Newsom, as a prime example of a “Silicon Valley Democrat”: “You don’t see him criticising these guys. He only goes after Trump, Trump, Trump and Vance, Vance, Vance … You want some viral content? Why don’t you go off on Peter Thiel’s weird antichrist obsession?” Even if the Democrats take control after the midterms or the 2028 presidential election, Durán is worried that “these tech fascists will win … because Democrats will not hold them accountable”.

On the plus side, the Silicon Valley takeover has not been going that well lately. Network states around the world are losing ground. In 2021, Próspera’s special economic status was repealed by the new president, Xiomara Castro (it is suing the Honduran government for $10.8bn). Two weeks ago, Srinivasan’s Network School was ordered to close (Srinivasan says he is moving it to Kazakhstan). Trump’s Freedom Cities remain unbuilt.

One saving grace, says Durán, is that “a lot of these people don’t really have a great grasp of on-the-ground realities”. Nobody really wants to live in a soulless network state, he says: “Why would you be in Kazakhstan instead of San Francisco, which is the global capital of tech?” On the other hand, he points out, the tech billionaires have effectively turned the US into a de facto network state.

But they may well have overplayed their hand. “Silicon Valley oligarchs are really vulnerable right now,” says Durán. “People don’t like them. People are starting to rise up against data centres and this vision of an AI apocalypse that kills all the jobs and potentially kills all of humanity. You’re scaring the hell out of people and now they don’t like you. Into that could step a politician to take advantage of that trend and come up with a message that speaks to the concerns of people and against the dark fantasies of the oligarchs.”

The question now, he says, “is how we turn the momentum in our favour and against the billionaires. Because they have a plan to win. They think they’re going to succeed.” This could be a radicalising moment: “In fighting against billionaire power, we find the key to all of our problems. Every moment is an important opportunity to wake people up and to start to fight back.”

If not, he says, we’ll find ourselves in a situation where “we don’t have democracy, we don’t have an economy and we don’t have a future. If that doesn’t radicalise people, then we deserve what we’re going to get.”

The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy is published on 18 August (Simon & Schuster, £25). To support the Guardian, buy a copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply

fullText:
AI Security Institute says models by OpenAI and Anthropic went rogue during a cybersecurity test and showed a new type of risk

Advanced AI models developed by OpenAI and Anthropic went rogue during a cybersecurity test and showed a new type of risk posed by the technology, according to the UK’s AI Security Institute.

AISI described the actions carried out by the agents – the term for AI systems that can perform tasks without human help – as a “serious incident”. In one example, an agent powered by Anthropic’s Mythos model sent targeted emails to people.

AISI said the rogue behaviour was carried out by agents powered by two models – Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol.

AISI said it detected unusual activity during a routine cybersecurity test for AI models on 28 July. It found that some of the agents had engaged in “sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations”. It took an hour to contain the incident.

In the most serious case, an agent powered by Mythos tried to insert malicious code into an open-source software project on GitHub, a platform used by software developers. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent then created fake online identities based on real people and used them to press the project’s overseer into accepting the code. These attempts were blocked by a human developer.

AISI said the agent used techniques commonly associated with real-world hackers. It sent emails to specifically chosen individuals – a technique known as “spear-phishing” – that attempted to manipulate the recipient. Some of the messages contained harmful software.

AISI said no harm was caused but the agents’ actions were unprecedented.

“This is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real world,” said AISI in a blogpost.

The incident followed recent similar episodes at OpenAI and Anthropic. In July, OpenAI said an agent powered by its models had hacked an AI startup during a test, and days later Anthropic said its Claude model had hacked three organisations during an evaluation.

AISI said the incident, taken alongside similar occurrences at OpenAI and Anthropic, represented a “shift in the risk landscape”. This was not an example of deliberate misuse of publicly available models, AISI said, but showed models in a research environment taking unintended action “beyond their authorised scope”.

AISI said 17 of the 19 cases of rogue behaviour that occurred during the evaluation were carried out by Mythos and two by Sol.

AISI said this was not a case of a model escaping its “sandbox”, or secure testing environment. The institute said it had intentionally permitted internet access and disabled filters within the models that blocked dangerous behaviour. The models are not publicly available in those operating conditions and there is no sign of such behaviour happening outside tests, AISI said.

The incident should be interpreted with “caution and nuance”, AISI said, but the signs of deceptive behaviour were “to an extent and severity we did not anticipate”. It was a small number of events that occurred under specific conditions, AISI added, but it had not happened before.

“What we can say is that the behaviour was possible, sustained and new. That alone warrants attention,” AISI said.

AISI admitted it was not actively monitoring the agents’ behaviour during the evaluation. It said it was putting tighter controls on internet access in tests as a result of the incident, introducing constant monitoring of tests and reassessing its design of tests. It said evaluations should assume a model would attempt to act beyond its remit.

The UK’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, said it was “absolutely vital” that the UK had a world-leading AI safety organisation. “Identifying new behaviour like this and sharing our findings, so we can tackle it, is exactly what AISI was set up to do,” he said.

OpenAI said the testing occurred during “conditions that do not reflect ordinary use”. An OpenAI spokesperson said: “We’ll continue working with evaluators and other stakeholders across the industry to strengthen shared practices for conducting evaluations safely as models become more capable.”

Anthropic said the incident “underscores the need for a broader conversation about how to safely evaluate increasingly capable AI agents” and it would continue to work with AISI on evaluating what happened.

fullText:
Company and subsidiary Statsig alleged by US justice department to have favored foreign workers in hiring

OpenAI and a subsidiary will pay $3.2m to settle US government claims that they ⁠favored foreign workers with temporary employment visas and discriminated against US job applicants in recruiting and hiring, the justice department said ⁠on Tuesday.

The justice ⁠department in ​a release said that OpenAI and Statsig, which makes product development software, recruited foreign workers for some open positions and ⁠took various steps to discourage US workers from applying.

That included requiring them to mail paper applications instead of submitting electronic ones, advertising jobs ⁠on the radio late at night, and not posting the openings on an external website, ​the justice department said.

OpenAI did ‌not immediately respond to ‌a request for comment. The company denied wrongdoing in the settlement agreement.

The justice department ‌has announced at least a dozen other settlements since last year in cases involving alleged discrimination against US workers, mostly by tech companies but none as high-profile as OpenAI.

Donald Trump has said that many companies abuse the temporary employment visa system and has sought to limit the hiring of foreign workers.

That has included imposing a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas for highly skilled workers, which are heavily utilized in the tech sector. The ​fee has been blocked pending legal challenges.

Assistant attorney general Harmeet Dhillon said in a statement that “this substantial settlement ensures that OpenAI redresses harm and changes its recruitment practices so US workers receive a fair opportunity for highly sought-after technology positions”.

The justice department alleged ⁠that both companies violated the federal Immigration and Nationality Act, which bars discrimination ​based on citizenship.

The ​department said that while there ​were fewer than 10 positions at issue, the sizeable settlement reflected the ​harm OpenAI’s conduct caused ‌to US ​workers.

The settlement includes $1.2m in penalties and $2m to compensate alleged victims of discrimination. OpenAI also agreed to revise its employment policies, conduct training, and to be subject to monitoring by the justice department, the agency said.

fullText:
Software group benefits from global systems and accounting practices ‘that enable tax to be shirked’, says union boss

The software group Palantir paid just £2m in corporation tax in the UK in 2024, despite holding public sector contracts worth hundreds of millions, thanks to tax breaks that are likely to reduce its contributions to governments around the world for years to come.

The US-headquartered company, which has harnessed AI to secure lucrative work for the NHS and the Ministry of Defence, is growing exponentially.

Palantir’s shares bounced 17% in early trading on Tuesday after its chief executive, Alex Karp, forecast worldwide revenues would almost double this year to $8bn (£5.95bn), a result that he described as “otherworldly”.

But the amount of tax Palantir pays compared to profits earned – its effective tax rate – is just 1.4% globally, according to a report published on Wednesday by the Centre for International Corporate Tax Accountability and Research (Cictar).

In the US last year, the company paid nothing in federal taxes and just over $2.5m in state taxes, the report states.

Andrea Egan, general secretary at the trade union Unison, which commissioned the report, said: “Systems that enable tax to be shirked on an industrial scale clearly have to change. The likes of Palantir need to stump up what’s due. Tech giants raking off billions in profit shouldn’t be free to pay what they please. Ministers shouldn’t award contracts to run public services to firms that are starving them of cash.”

The UK is Palantir’s biggest market outside the US, with £247m of revenues declared by the company for 2024, the most recent year covered by the report, while the majority of its non-US workforce – about 750 employees – are based in Britain.

As of 2026, Palantir holds an estimated £670m in government contracts. A three-year, £240m deal with the MoD was awarded last December without a competitive tender.

In 2024 the company paid just £2.1m in UK corporation tax, despite declaring profits of over £25m, giving an effective tax rate of just over 8%, researchers found. The UK corporation tax rate was 25% that year and remains at that level.

Despite the size of the UK market, tax collected here was less than in South Korea, Japan, France or Germany.

One reason, according to the researchers, is that Palantir is accounting for its UK revenues in the US, a practice sometimes referred to as transfer pricing. “A major pattern emerges of Palantir shifting revenues and profits from contracts in Europe to the US parent company to take advantage of the massive tax shelter it has created there,” they said.

While 26% of all Palantir revenue is sourced from customers outside the US, only 4% of revenue is booked abroad. The reason for this is not clear, but researchers said they believed contracts with customers were signed with Palantir’s US companies, which in turn paid a service fee to local country subsidiaries to deliver the work.

For example, Palantir disclosed £159m of revenues in its UK company filings for 2024, but disclosed £247m of UK revenues in its stock market filings.

A spokesperson for Palantir said the company complied with the tax regimes in the jurisdictions in which it operated, and criticising its use of transfer pricing was “simply not credible”. They said: “Transfer pricing, which allocates a company’s profits among entities within the Palantir group of companies, is an entirely standard practice that is virtually universal for large multinational companies.”

They said accounting practices could lead to different filings in different countries, and it was common for US parent companies, as the ultimate owners of the products sold, to record revenues earned abroad.

Another way in which Palantir cuts its tax bill is by granting share options to staff. The company can reduce what it owes by the amount the shares are worth when they vest. Employees are liable for income tax on their share options, often at higher rates, but the use of shares rather than cash to pay staff shifts the tax burden from the company to its employees.

A Palantir spokesperson said this was “a completely standard tax measure established under the previous Labour government [in the UK]”, designed to give employees a real stake in a business. “Crucially, it means that more tax is paid because corporation tax is 25%, whereas for these shares, income tax, which is higher, is due.”

In the US, Palantir has stored up billions in tax credits from share options, and losses carried forward from previous years, meaning that at the current rate of profit, it would not be liable for US federal income tax payments for “nearly a decade”, the report states.

Like other US companies, Palantir is also a beneficiary of tax cuts implemented under Donald Trump, who reduced the rate for corporations from 35% to 21% during his first term as president. In his second term, he negotiated a carve-out from an international agreement to impose a minimum tax rate of 15% on large multinationals.

“While profits are earned in European markets, much of that income is returned to the US in the form of related party payments,” the report states. “While some level of related party payments may be justified, it appears that Palantir’s efforts are intentionally and artificially reducing taxable income and income tax payments across its European operations.”

Palantir said it paid $148m in UK employment taxes last year, a figure that included employer national insurance contributions and some income tax paid on behalf of staff.

title: AI-generated stories rated better quality than human-written ones, study finds
description: Researcher says simpler writing by AI is easier to read and digest, but this does not mean human authors are obsolete
fullText:
Researcher says simpler writing by AI is easier to read and digest, but this does not mean human authors are obsolete

From Homer’s Odyssey to Agatha Christie’s crime fiction, humans have produced plenty of tales to grace the bookshelf. But research suggests artificial intelligence may now be providing some competition.

In a study published in the journal Judgment and Decision Making, 1,682 adults were asked to read one of six short stories, three of which were written by humans and three by ChatGPT. Each AI story had a similar theme to one of the human-authored works.

The team told participants whether their story was written by a human or AI, but this information was not always correct. The researchers then asked participants to rate how absorbing and engaging they found the story, and its quality.

Participants who read an AI-generated story rated it as more absorbing and of higher quality than those who read a story written by a human. However, participants gave higher ratings to stories they had been told were written by people.

Dr Deena Skolnick Weisberg, a senior author of the research from Villanova University in Pennsylvania, said: “AI systems can already generate short stories that are seen as being at least as good as – if not better than – human-written stories. We should update our views of AI’s abilities accordingly.”

However, Weisberg, who is herself a creative writer, said that did not mean writing should be left to AI, noting that novels produced by tech were probably going to be different from those written by humans.

“We may need to make room for AI-generated novels, and for AI/human co-written novels, but that doesn’t mean that there’s no longer space for us to appreciate the process of human creativity,” she said.

“Humans write as a form of creative self-expression or to challenge ourselves, or to make sense of our experiences. The fact that AI can generate human-like stories doesn’t change any of that.”

The results also suggest attitudes to AI matter: participants with more positive attitudes toward AI gave higher ratings to stories they were told were produced by ChatGPT than those with a less positive outlook.

The researchers carried out two further experiments in which 905 adults were given two of the six short stories – both on the same theme and only one of which was penned by a person. They were then asked to guess which was written by a human and which by AI.

In one experiment, about 40% guessed correctly, a result that is worse than chance, while in the other experiment 52% guessed correctly.

“There is no general evidence that participants were able to distinguish human-written from AI-generated stories,” the authors write.

The researchers found that while participants’ self-reported expertise with fiction was not linked to how accurately they guessed, greater expertise with AI systems was.

“AI writing has a particular style that we can learn to recognise with practice – just as we can learn to recognise different human authors’ unique styles,” Weisberg said.

Weisberg suggested that the preference for stories labelled as being written by humans was linked to a desire for authenticity, but that people actually preferred AI-generated stories because they were easier to read and digest.

However, Luke Kennard, a professor of film and creative writing at the University of Birmingham, who was not involved in the work, emphasised that AI was highly contentious.

“Because we’re human, we tend to personify AI and imagine it as some kind of glowing robot with a benign and neutral face, when it’s really just predictive code based on a massive stolen database of actual writing, physically based in vast, expensive and destructive datacentres with catastrophic repercussions for the surrounding communities,” he said.

Kennard also stressed that AI was not a “tool” similar to spellcheck or a thesaurus, but an existential threat.

“Of course it’s capable of spitting out a coherent and even enjoyable poem with the right prompting and finessing. Given that it’s been trained on thousands of years of human work, it would be embarrassing if it wasn’t,” he said. “I suppose the question we should be asking is: is it worth it? And the answer is absolutely, categorically, it is not.”
